findings.title: Communication scale contradiction

The direction of the error is undetermined: either the response options are misdescribed, or the '5' is a typo for '4'. Related but weaker: 3.83 is glossed as corresponding to 'good', yet on the paper's own labels 3 = Good and 4 = Outstanding, so 3.83 sit

findings.title: T2 constant p below attainable (Table 2, Constant, model 1 (communication))
findings.description: The entire rounding interval implied by the printed coefficient and SE gives p between .0025 and .0028 -- roughly 2.5 to 2.8 times the claimed threshold, and nowhere near <.001. The mismatch survives a sensitivity check on the reference distribution: under a small-sample t with df=57 the p rises further to .0039, so no choice of reference distribution rescues '<.001'. Kept at `suspicious` rather than `impossible` because this is a p-threshold LABEL on a model intercept, not a substantive claim; a mis-mapped significance marker is the most economical explanation. df=100000 was used as a numerically exact stand-in for the normal reference distribution Stata uses for Poisson models.

findings.title: Ctc text vs table discrepancy (Results paragraph 4 vs Table 3, Communities That Care)
findings.description: Per rulebook rule 10, the discrepancy itself is the finding. Recomputation from the most primitive numbers available (the coefficient and SE) adjudicates in favour of the text: p is about .0013, which satisfies p<.01 but not p<.001. So the Table 3 entry is the erroneous one. Low substantive impact -- CTC is a covariate, not a study hypothesis -- but it is a second instance of the same failure mode as t2_constant_p_below_attainable, and the co-occurrence is what makes the pattern worth reporting.

findings.title: T3 identical inputs different p (Table 3, Number of EBP at baseline, models 1 and 3)
findings.description: Two cells print an IDENTICAL coefficient and standard error but carry p-values differing by more than four orders of magnitude (.01 vs <.001). IMPORTANT CAVEAT AGAINST OVER-READING: the coefficient is rounded to 2 decimals while the SE is given to 3, so the true ratio is very poorly pinned -- a coefficient anywhere in [.005, .015] against SE .002 spans t from 2.5 to 7.5, which covers both reported p-values. findings.title: Multiplicity uncorrected (Analyses section; Tables 2, 3 and 4)
findings.description: Nine primary tests are reported with no correction mentioned anywhere. Five reach p<.05, and four of those sit in the .01-.03 band, which is where an uncorrected family of nine would be most vulnerable. Compounding this, covariates were selected by pre-screening bivariate associations at p<0.10 on the same data, a data-dependent model-building step whose effect on the reported p-values is not accounted for. Neither practice is unusual in this literature and neither makes any individual number wrong; the point is that the nominal p-values understate the false-positive risk across the family, and the paper offers no adjustment or acknowledgement.

findings.title: Randomisation baseline not reportable (Methods, sample description; Table 1)
findings.description: Recorded explicitly because the baseline-similarity checks are normally the highest-yield tests on a randomised design, and their absence here would otherwise read as a silent gap. Randomisation was by COALITION (a cluster), which means csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion would in any case refuse or be capped -- cluster allocation breaks the independence both methods assume. So there is no baseline-uniformity finding in this paper, in either direction, and none should be inferred. Table 1 pools all 64 coalitions into a single column, so the trial's allocation is not verifiable from what is printed.
